By Elissa Sanci

Elissa Sanci is a senior writer who has reported on label makers, tumblers, and more. She once dumped glitter in her car to test handheld vacuums.

This season’s most talked-about French accessory isn’t a designer bag or belt, but a leather notebook: the Louise Carmen Roadbook.

A trifold, leather-bound, fully customizable notebook, the Roadbook has become something of a status symbol. Starting at €132 (around $150) and going up to over €400 (roughly $460), Louise Carmen’s offerings are definitively luxury. Whether you’re online or at the Louise Carmen boutique in Paris, you can customize everything from the color of the leather and elastic closures to the added adornments like embossed initials and unique charms.

The Roadbook falls into a category of notebooks called traveler’s notebooks — a concept first popularized by Traveler’s Company in 2006 with the $60 Traveler’s Notebook, a top pick in our guide to the best planners. Unlike traditional notebooks with pages sewn into the spine, traveler-style notebooks are simple leather folios that hold separate thin notebooks inside. These notebooks, called inserts, are held in place inside the reusable cover with elastic bands, allowing you to swap, combine, and rearrange them over time. And because the inserts are interchangeable, the idea is that a traveler’s notebook should last a lifetime.

As the Roadbook has exploded in popularity along with a general trend toward analog routines and hobbies, another brand has been coming up in conversation: Paper Republic, a company based in Vienna, Austria, that offers similarly customizable, luxe leather journals. At $85, the Grand Voyageur XL is a fraction of the cost of a Roadbook — and, according to some #JournalTok enthusiasts, equally as sophisticated.

At a glance, these three brands of notebooks — Louise Carmen, Traveler’s Company, and Paper Republic — can look quite different, varying in leather, finish, and price, but structurally, they’re nearly identical. In most cases, you’re paying for a piece of leather, a few elastic loops, and a customizable setup.

Even though I’m a sucker for a beautiful notebook, I didn’t think that spending more money on a journal would meaningfully improve the experience of using one. So over the last two months, I used each of these three notebooks daily to journal, take notes at work, keep track of my monthly plans, jot down my daily to-do list, and even collage and junk-journal. I carried the journals around in my backpack, crammed them into small purses, and used them in a variety of locations, including sticky bar tops and damp park picnic tables. I even left the notebooks out in direct sunlight, spilled water on them, and scratched the covers with my keys to test durability of the leather, cringing the entire time.

After I subjected both the luxe and humble options to the gauntlet of daily life, one thing became obvious: The ultimate traveler’s notebook isn’t the one with the most prestige. It’s the one you’re not afraid to use.

Spilled water, uncapped pens, the wrong side of a sharp key — your everyday notebook should be tough enough to weather whatever the world throws its way. The Traveler’s Notebook is up for the challenge.

This planner is a cross between a simple calendar and a beautiful journal. And you can fill it with a range of inserts for any type of planning.

The Traveler’s Notebook stands in comparison with the Louise Carmen Roadbook, which has a more sophisticated, luxurious look. The Roadbook’s leather is remarkably thin and supple, giving it a flexible, almost delicate feel, and the patina is striking in person.

The Traveler’s Notebook, on the other hand, is made of thicker, stiffer leather that scuffs more easily — but this gives the journal a durable, rugged feel that makes it better suited to everyday use. I didn’t feel the need to be as gentle with the Traveler’s Notebook, which made me want to reach for it more often than the Roadbook, and I never felt guilty tossing my Traveler’s Notebook into my backpack.

The Traveler’s Notebook, which is an A5 slim size, is chunkier than the Roadbook, giving it a less refined look. The leather folio folds in half rather than wrapping around the inserts, leaving the notebook edges exposed, and the spine only has one elastic band; this means you’ll need to use an extra elastic loop if you want to add three inserts (sold separately), and the notebooks don’t stack quite as nicely on top of each other when the journal cover is closed. And at first, the stiffer leather doesn’t lie flat, which makes writing in the notebooks a bit frustrating. But the spine softens over time with use.

The Louise Carmen Roadbook’s elegant trifold design, on the other hand, comfortably holds three notebook inserts. Each insert is secured to the spine by its own elastic bands so they can stack neatly atop each other within the leather folio, which wraps protectively around the notebooks. This gives the journal a sleek, sophisticated look when it’s closed and allows the leather to lie flat when it’s open, making the inserts easier to use.

The Traveler’s Notebook is considerably cheaper than any Louise Carmen offering. My bespoke Roadbook (prune-colored leather with a bright orange elastic closure and two charms on the spine) came to a whopping €240 after taxes and shipping. The Traveler’s Company Traveler’s Notebook Starter Kit — which includes the leather cover, a blank notebook, and a spare elastic band — is $60. Notebook inserts are around $5 a piece, bringing the total for a Traveler’s Notebook with three inserts to about $70.

Additionally, Traveler’s Company offers the most extensive range of inserts (most of which are under $10), and despite the unique size, they’re relatively easy to find from third-party sellers as well.

Is the Louise Carmen Roadbook nicer than the Traveler’s Notebook? Undoubtedly. But for a notebook that’s meant to be thrown in a bag and taken everywhere (inevitably getting banged up in the process), we can’t justify the price difference and would choose the Traveler’s Notebook every time.

The Traveler’s Notebook’s rugged look and unique dimensions aren’t for everyone. If you’re drawn to Louise Carmen journals because of their sleek, sophisticated aesthetic, the Paper Republic Grand Voyageur XL might satisfy that itch at a more affordable price point.

This bifold leather folio is a great middle ground between the rugged Traveler’s Notebook and high-end luxury brands. It easily holds up to three inserts (including standard A5 notebooks) and lies flat for long writing sessions. While its edges can curl over time and the bifold design leaves your page edges exposed, its durability, elegant look, and travel-friendly versatility make it an exceptional value.

The Grand Voyageur XL is comparable in size and overall look to the Roadbook. Both feel refined and design-forward, can comfortably hold three notebook inserts, and easily lie flat while in use.

Where they diverge is structure: The Roadbook uses three elastics to hold multiple inserts in place, while Paper Republic opts for a simpler, single-elastic system similar to the Traveler’s Notebook. And like the Traveler’s Notebook, the Grand Voyageur XL is a bifold leather folio that leaves the edges of the inserts exposed.

The Paper Republic notebook inserts are slightly smaller than standard A5 notebooks, though I found that A5 inserts, like the Moleskine Cahier Journals, also fit comfortably within the cover. Both the leather cover and the inserts open flat easily and stay that way, making them particularly pleasant for longer writing sessions and more visual, artsy use.

The Grand Voyageur XL is made of vachetta leather, a vegetable-tanned cowhide known for its soft, natural finish. It’s slightly thicker and more structured than the ultra-thin leather used by Louise Carmen, yet it’s more flexible than the sturdier hide of the Traveler’s Notebook. The result is a middle ground: supple and pliable, but with a bit more durability. This leather held up particularly well to the woes of everyday life; editor Hannah Rimm spilled a can of seltzer on her Paper Republic notebook and saw nearly no change to the leather after wiping it dry.

The leather’s flexibility, however, comes with trade-offs. Over time, the corners tend to curl, and the elastic closure can leave visible indentations in the leather. I didn’t find this particularly bothersome — it adds to the journal’s worn-in character — but Hannah, who also tested the Grand Voyageur XL, was less forgiving. “Aesthetically, I don’t love the way the edges curl up,” she said, “And unless I always keep a lot of sturdy notebooks in it, I can tell the curling will get worse with time.”

The Grand Voyageur XL strikes a nice balance between the sophistication of the Roadbook and the practicality of the Traveler’s Notebook, making it an appealing option if you want something that looks just as good but feels a bit more durable for everyday use.

It’s also significantly cheaper than the Roadbook: the Grand Voyageur XL journal is $80 and includes one notebook insert. Additional Paper Republic standard refill inserts are $19 for a set of two, bringing the full bundle to around $100. The company also offers embossing for only an additional $3 — and while it doesn’t offer an array of charms, adding your own charms is easy to do (and much cheaper than the charm offerings from Louise Carmen).

Equal parts elegant and practical, the Grand Voyageur XL would also make a beautiful gift, and it’s an excellent travel companion. The roomy cover can easily accommodate multiple notebooks and travel documents — and it can even fit a Kindle e-reader, as long as it’s in a case with a cover.

On #JournalTok, a growing number of crafty creators who admire Louise Carmen notebooks but balk at the prices have started making their own versions. The appeal is obvious: For a fraction of the cost, you can make a journal fully customized to your exact needs.

But the idea of working with leather was daunting to me. So I turned to writer and textile expert Alex Aciman, who quickly assuaged my fears. “Something like a notebook cover only requires four cuts, and doesn’t require stitching or joining multiple pieces,” he told me. “It’s not hard and doesn’t require a lot of tools, but it does take a few thoughtful operations and some creative considerations, so it’s rewarding.”

To make a traveler’s journal, you only need a handful of supplies: a panel of leather, a leather hole puncher, eyelets and washers, an eyelet setter, and elastic cord. You also need a cutting mat, a ruler, a hammer, a utility knife, pliers, and a lighter to burnish the edges after cutting. I was able to buy all of these supplies for about $20 on Amazon. I then spent $30 on a panel of 3-ounce leather from Tandy Leather, and I was off to the races.

Following a tutorial by creator Jananie Velu, I made three covers (with enough leftover to make two more), bringing the cost of each journal to roughly $10.

Once I got the hang of it, I was ready to step up my game and make a Louise Carmen dupe. Alex suggested I use buttero leather to match the look and feel of the Roadbook, and I was able to find a 9-by-16-inch piece of this luxurious leather for $25.

Making the journal took me less than 20 minutes. It’s not perfect — the bottom edge is slightly askew, and the grommets along the spine are a bit too close together — but those small flaws are what make it uniquely mine. It feels like something I made, not something I bought. And functionally, it is exactly the same as the Louise Carmen Roadbook, for a 10th of the price.

Making your own traveler’s notebook isn’t for everyone. But if you’re willing to experiment (and accept a few imperfections), it’s easily the most cost-effective way to create a journaling system tailored to your specific needs.

After testing the Louise Carmen Roadbook, the Traveler’s Company Traveler’s Notebook, and the Paper Republic Grand Voyageur XL, and even making my own, one thing was clear. The best traveler’s notebook isn’t necessarily the most beautiful or the most expensive, it’s the one that works best for your specific needs. And whether you buy one or make it yourself, the appeal isn’t just in how it looks, but how it evolves with you over time.

This article was edited by Hannah Rimm and Maxine Builder.

Elissa Sanci
